name: Shotgun House

revival_periods.note: The shotgun returns as a small-lot infill and cottage-court type in New Urbanist and post-Katrina rebuilding practice, where its 14-foot width and front-porch social logic solve exactly the problems that produced it.

lineage.note: The New Orleans building trade that produced the shotgun was the Creole trade: the same carpenters, the same cypress, the same hall-less planning logic in which rooms open directly into one another and circulation happens outdoors. ACKNOWLEDGED GAP: the West African (Yoruba) and Haitian ti kay ancestry described at length in this node has no target node in the taxonomy, so the graph currently understates it. The resolved cascade is Franco-Norman only and should be read with that caveat until an African/Caribbean trunk exists.
French colonial framing practice (briquette-entre-poteaux, cypress sills, full-width galleries) supplied the construction system into which the African-Caribbean plan was built.

Later shotguns borrow raised-floor and gallery details from the region's higher-status buildings, and after 1880 borrow Italianate and Eastlake millwork brackets wholesale, without descending from either.

description.short: A house one room wide and three to five rooms deep, gable and porch to the street, its doors aligned on a single axis - a New Orleans type with documented West African and Haitian plan antecedents, not an Anglo economization of a narrow lot.
description.long:
The shotgun is a plan before it is anything else: a single file of rooms, each twelve to fourteen feet square, opening directly into the next with no hallway, the whole strung front to back on a narrow deep lot with the gable end and a porch turned to the street. Three rooms is the minimum, five is common, and the rooms are typically parlour, bedroom, bedroom, kitchen in sequence, so that reaching the last room means passing through every private space in the house. The doors align on one axis, which is the ventilation strategy - open the front and back doors on a July night and the whole house becomes a single duct - and which also produced, at some point in the later nineteenth century, the folk etymology that gives the type its name. The camelback variant adds a second storey only over the rear rooms, preserving the one-storey street reading and, not incidentally, the property tax assessment that went with it.

The origins are the substance of this node, because the popular explanation is wrong and the scholarship correcting it is solid. The folk account says the shotgun is simply the cheapest way to fit a house on a narrow lot taxed by frontage. That is true as far as it goes and explains nothing distinctive: narrow lots exist everywhere and produced side-hall townhouses in Philadelphia, back-to-backs in Manchester and railroad flats in New York, none of which look like this. John Michael Vlach's work of the mid-1970s - his 1975 dissertation and the two-part 1976 Pioneer America article 'The Shotgun House: An African Architectural Legacy' - traced the plan to the Yoruba two-room house of West Africa, roughly twelve by twenty feet with the entrance in the gable end, carried to Saint-Domingue in the slave trade, where it fused with Arawak and French Caribbean building to produce the Haitian ti kay. The transmission event is documented: between 1809 and 1810 roughly ten thousand refugees from the Haitian Revolution - white planters, free people of colour, and enslaved people in nearly equal thirds - arrived in New Orleans by way of Cuba, doubling the city's population. Jay Edwards has since identified some 140 linear cottages in New Orleans built before 1840. The name may itself be African: Vlach proposed the Fon word to-gun, 'place of assembly', reaching English through Louisiana Creole, which would make the shotgun-through-the-doors story a later folk rationalisation of a word nobody recognised. Not every claim in this chain is equally secure - the etymology is the weakest link and Edwards has argued for a more complex Creole synthesis than a single African line - but the central point survives all of the criticism: the shotgun is a Black architectural tradition that arrived in North America through the Caribbean, and calling it a poor man's cottage erases the only interesting thing about it.

The conditions that made it a mass type are industrial and post-emancipation. From the 1860s the shotgun became the standard rental and owner-built house for Black urban communities across the South and, with the Great Migration, into Louisville, Memphis, Houston, and industrial towns as far as Los Angeles; thousands were built in New Orleans in the 1880s and 1890s alone. Mill-sawn cypress and pine, machine-cut nails and catalogue millwork made it fast and cheap to build; a builder could produce a row of them on a single subdivided lot. It absorbed whatever ornament the era offered - Italianate brackets, Eastlake spindlework, Queen Anne gable shingles - all of it concentrated on the street gable and the porch, because that eight feet of frontage was the entire public face of the household. Its subsequent history is a story of policy: shotgun neighbourhoods were redlined, cleared for urban renewal and interstate construction, and after 2005 flooded and demolished in enormous numbers, so the surviving stock is a fraction of what was built.

Standing on the porch of one, the first thing you notice is that the porch is the room the house does not otherwise have. It is five to eight feet deep, full width, raised two or three feet above the banquette, and it faces a street of identical porches four feet away across a narrow yard - a social machine of extraordinary efficiency, and the reason former residents describe the type in terms of neighbours rather than rooms. Inside, the axis is the whole experience: standing at the front door you see straight through four doorways and out the back, a hundred and twenty feet of aligned openings, and the ceilings are ten to twelve feet so the volume feels far larger than the fourteen-foot width. There is no privacy in the modern sense and there was never meant to be; the plan assumes that circulation happens on the porch and in the yard, exactly as it does in the West African compound and the Caribbean village the plan came from.

defining_characteristics: One room wide, three to five rooms deep, with no hallway - rooms open directly into one another in an enfilade
Front and rear doors and all intervening doors aligned on a single longitudinal axis
Gable end turned to the street, with a full-width porch under or attached to the front gable
House width of 12-16 feet overall, set by the room, not by the lot
Ceiling heights of 10-12 feet, disproportionate to the plan width, for stack ventilation in a subtropical climate
Ornament concentrated entirely on the street gable and porch, whatever the current millwork catalogue offered
Growth by adding rooms to the rear, or by the camelback: a second storey over the rear rooms only
diagnostic_tells: Sight line straight through the house from the front door to the back door - no other American type does this
Front facade of one or two openings only, a door and a window, under a gable
Porch full width and at least 5 feet deep, raised on brick or cypress piers with an open crawl beneath
Camelback profile: a house that is one storey from the street and two from the alley
Rows of identical units at 3-6 foot spacings on subdivided lots, sharing a rhythm but not party walls

distinguished_from.difference: The Creole cottage faces the street broadside with four openings, no centred door, and a hall-less four-room plan two rooms deep. The shotgun turns ninety degrees and goes to one room wide. They share carpenters, cypress, ceiling heights and the refusal of interior corridors.

A massing, not a style, and much broader. A Greek Revival or Folk Victorian gable-front house is two or three bays wide with a side hall; the shotgun is one room wide with no hall at all. Width and the absence of a passage are the test.

Different ancestry and different climate logic. The farmhouse is Anglo-descended, two rooms deep or more, has a central or side passage, and grows by ell. The shotgun is Afro-Caribbean in plan, single-file, and grows only backward.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Governed by the room and by airflow. Width is one room, depth is a repeated module, and ceiling height is set by stack ventilation rather than by any proportional canon; the street gable is proportioned by the porch.
typical_ratios: Overall width 12-16 feet; individual rooms 11-14 feet square
Ceiling height 10-12 feet, giving a room whose height nearly equals its width
Porch depth 5-8 feet, full width; floor raised 18-36 inches above grade on piers
Roof pitch 6:12 to 10:12 front-gabled; camelback rear section 1.5-2 storeys
Lot frontage 25-32 feet with 4-8 feet of side yard, from the New Orleans standard 30 x 120 foot lot
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Street facade of two openings (door and window) or three on a double shotgun; the side elevation carries one window per room at even spacing, which is the plan module made visible.

massing_affinities.note: The type and the massing are the same object.
Wider gable-front cottages of two rooms' width are a related but distinct type and should not be labelled shotgun.
Shares the region and the builders but not the plan; the four-opening broadside face is the opposite move.

constraints.statement: All door openings must align on a single longitudinal axis within 3 inches, front door to rear door. Offsetting an interior door breaks the ventilation path that is the type's entire environmental strategy.
Overall width 12-16 feet, one room wide throughout, with no interior hallway. A hall added down one side converts the building to a side-hall cottage and is a different type.

test.note: Tests the overall width range (12-16ft) via facade_width_ft, the narrow gable end that addresses the street. 'No interior hallway' is also cleanly testable via corridor_present = 'no' but is left as prose here since the schema allows one test per constraint.

constraints.statement: Ceiling height minimum 10 feet (11-12 typical), with a transom over every interior door and operable windows on both side walls of every room. The section is the cooling system.

test.note: Tests the 10ft minimum ceiling height. The interior-door-transom requirement and the two-side operable-window rule are left as prose.

constraints.statement: Full-width front porch of at least 5 feet depth (6-8 preferred), raised 18-36 inches above grade. The porch is the house's only social space and its only public face; a shotgun without one is incomplete rather than merely plain.

test.note: Tests the minimum full-width porch depth (5ft) via gallery_depth_ft. The raised-floor height above grade (18-36in, testable via floor_height_above_grade_in) is left as prose here since the schema allows one test per constraint.

constraints.statement: Growth is to the rear only. A camelback second storey must begin at least two rooms back from the front wall so the street elevation remains single-storey; a full second storey over the front rooms destroys the type.

exemplars.name: Elvis Presley Birthplace
exemplars.note: Built by Vernon Presley; a two-room wood-frame shotgun with a hipped roof and a front porch on thin wooden posts. The irreducible minimum version of the type, and precisely dated.
exemplars.why: The one any reader names first, standing on its original site; and the only example in this node whose construction is precisely dated, by the $180 Vernon Presley borrowed for materials in 1934 on the owner's own account. CORRECTED 5 Sep 2026 by the cluster audit: this had said 'dated to the day', and no source read dates the building to a day -- the loan dates it to a year; and 'the most visited two-room shotgun in the world' was withdrawn, since no page in the record counts visitors.

exemplars.name: Shotgun House (Santa Monica Conservancy Preservation Resource Center)
exemplars.location: 2712 Second Street (original site), Ocean Park, Santa Monica, California
exemplars.note: Three rooms in line, board-and-batten, front porch, with Queen Anne shingling on the street gable - evidence of the type's migration to the Pacific Coast as worker and resort housing. Relocated 2014, opened as a preservation centre 2016.
exemplars.why: The Pacific Coast expression, and the case that tests the node's own account of the type: built in 1897 as a seaside vacation cottage 'just two blocks from the Santa Fe railroad depot in Ocean Park', which is neither the Southern rental history nor the industrial one, and which is the Conservancy's own history page. The 468 sq ft is the Santa Monica Daily Press's figure, not the Conservancy's, and is the only floor area anyone has published for the building. CORRECTED 5 Sep 2026 by the cluster audit, which found the area and the history attributed to one page that carries only the history.

exemplars.name: Faubourg Marigny and Bywater shotgun rows
exemplars.note: The densest surviving concentration of the type, mostly 1880s-1890s, single and double shotguns and camelbacks with Italianate and Eastlake millwork on the street gables. Cited as a district because the individually documented early examples largely did not survive.
exemplars.why: Cited as a district because the National Register nomination for Bywater counts the type instead of admiring it - 61% of the district's building stock is shotgun houses, 3% camelbacks, and 47% of the shotguns are singles - which is the only quantitative statement about the type in this corpus.

exemplars.name: Kuntz Shotgun House
exemplars.location: 1401 East Washington Street, Louisville, Jefferson County, Kentucky
exemplars.note: A brick camelback of 1889-91 with three rooms back to back perpendicular to the street and a fourth over the rear one, recorded by HABS with reduced copies of measured drawings. Its data form's SHAPE AND DIMENSIONS field is blank, so the survey states the room count and no dimension at all.
exemplars.why: The only measured federal record of a shotgun house this cluster could reach, and the survey types it itself - 'This is a typical "shotgun" house' - which is what makes it a specimen rather than an illustration.

exemplars.name: 1812 West Muhammad Ali Boulevard (House)
exemplars.location: 1812 West Muhammad Ali Boulevard, Russell National Register District, Louisville, Jefferson County, Kentucky
exemplars.note: A single-storey brick Italianate single shotgun in the Russell district, its facade later faced in form stone, with segmentally arched hoods over a two-bay front and a sawn wood Gothic bargeboard cornice. HABS dates the type and not the house - 'the late 19th and early 20th centuries' - so the year is left null.
exemplars.why: Plain, surveyed and useful because it is ordinary: a federal survey stating that the type was 'routinely built for the common man as worker housing' and that the ornament of the day was applied to it, which is this node's argument about the street gable in a government document.

exemplars.name: Project Row Houses
exemplars.note: Twenty-two derelict shotgun houses of about 1930 at Holman and Live Oak, bought in 1993 by Rick Lowe and six other artists rather than let the city clear them; now five blocks and some thirty-nine buildings. The founder's own account names John Biggers and the West African-Caribbean derivation of the plan as the reason.
exemplars.why: The group by which the type's African and Caribbean ancestry entered public consciousness, and the reason the shotgun is now argued about rather than cleared; the judgment rests on the founder's own statement of why these houses and not others were saved.

sources: John Michael Vlach, 'The Shotgun House: An African Architectural Legacy', Pioneer America 8 (1976), parts 1 and 2
John Michael Vlach, Sources of the Shotgun House: African and Caribbean Antecedents for Afro-American Architecture (PhD dissertation, Indiana University, 1975)
Jay D. Edwards, 'Shotgun: The Most Contested House in America', Buildings & Landscapes 16 (2009)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2013)
64 Parishes (Louisiana Endowment for the Humanities), 'Shotgun House'

proportion_packs.note: The closest available match for the shotgun's 11-14 ft enfilade rooms and 10-12 ft stack-ventilation ceilings, offered with an explicit caveat rather than as a clean fit: room-vernacular's module is reconstructed from Anglo-American measured fabric, and this node's own lineage entry flags the shotgun's real plan ancestry -- a documented West African (Yoruba) and Haitian antecedent -- as an 'ACKNOWLEDGED GAP' in this taxonomy with no target node of its own. The physical constraints room-vernacular reconstructs (joist span, daylight depth, a hearth or stove's reach) are constraints of physics rather than of any one building culture, so the numbers plausibly transfer even though the plan-generating logic does not. What does NOT transfer is the room_adjacency_overrides rule's direction: the shotgun's rooms are strung front-to-back along the depth of a one-room-wide lot rather than tiled across a frontage, the reverse of every Anglo type the pack was built from.

Bound narrowly, for one thing only: the type's hard constraint that every interior door carries an operable transom (c03) is exactly the ventilation-transom device this pack's window-head notes describe, and its transom_sidelight rule -- that a transom must take the same light module as the windows it is glazed with, 'because they came out of the same box of glass and the same joiner's shop' -- is a free internal-consistency check across the street gable's one or two openings and the interior transom run. Not bound for light-count dating: the type's ornamental era (Italianate and Eastlake catalog millwork, mostly 1880s-1890s) is already carried by the node's own description and constraints, and forcing a divided-light pattern onto what were commonly large 1/1 or 2/2 panes by that date would misdate the building.

Optional. The shotgun's full-width front porch takes turned posts, brackets and a valance from the same catalogues as everything else in this family, and this node is thinly bound. What the pack cannot say here is anything about how much: the same house appears with a full spindled porch and with four plain posts, and the difference is the owner's money in the year it was built rather than a rule.

declined_packs.reason: The pack's own module is "One dressed stone: the bed height a banker mason cuts a quoin, jamb or lintel to", and its module note says outright that it proportions THE DRESSINGS -- quoin, jamb, lintel, mullion, kneeler, coping -- and treats the rubble field as what is left over. It therefore presupposes a wall of stone laid by a waller with dressings cut at a banker. The shotgun's record names its own construction and it is milled softwood carpentry with machine-cut nails and catalogue millwork; the only masonry anywhere in the record is the alternative pier under the porch floor ("raised on brick or cypress piers"), which is a foundation and not a wall. A pack that begins at the banker mason's bench has nothing in this building to dimension.
declined_packs.quote: Mill-sawn cypress and pine, machine-cut nails and catalogue millwork made it fast and cheap to build
declined_packs.note: Measured --impact: governs 9 slots. Eight re-attribute -- belt_course to vignola-composite (roman-classical); corner_quoin, height_proportion and wing_strategy to timber-bay (french-provincial-farmhouse); daylight_strategy and depth_and_pile to room-vernacular (the node's own binding); foundation_expression to facade-peristyle (roman-classical); window_proportion to sash-light (the node's own binding). roof_material loses all dimensioning. CAVEAT: --impact measures one decline at a time, and timber-bay is declined in this same pass, so corner_quoin, height_proportion and wing_strategy will fall past it to whatever is next or to nothing.

declined_packs.reason: timber-bay's module is one structural bay -- bent centre to bent centre -- at sixteen to twenty feet, bounded above by the span a hewn 4 x 8 in joist will make, and its own note states the test: can you draw the frame, and if the plan does not resolve into bays of 16 to 20 feet the building is wearing a costume. The shotgun's record names its own module and it is the room: the whole house is 12-16 ft wide, and its repeated rooms are 11-14 ft square, so the entire building is narrower than one of this pack's bays. The record also describes a mill-sawn, machine-nailed construction rather than the hewn box frame the bay is reckoned from. This is a rival module rather than a coincident figure -- the inverse of the timber-bay trap, where a 16-20 ft log pen agrees in number and not in mechanism.
declined_packs.quote: House width of 12-16 feet overall, set by the room, not by the lot
declined_packs.note: Measured --impact: governs 3 slots and NONE loses dimensioning -- chimney to corbel-course (french-provincial-farmhouse), eave_condition to trim-sawn (the node's own binding), roof_pitch to balcony-gallery (creole-cottage-vernacular). It also absorbs three slots from the stone-course decline above, which will now fall past it. --pair reports that ENDORSING would arm a live check: span_check via _timber_bay_applies_to, and the CP model reading the same list, switch span capacity from the light-frame joist table to the bay module's own. Declining arms nothing and leaves the light-frame table in place, which is what "mill-sawn cypress and pine, machine-cut nails" describes.
